findings.title: Google credential key is overwritten with a zod SafeParseReturnType wrapper object
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the full zod safeParse result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed token. In `refreshAccessToken` the return value is assigned to `key` and written directly with `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. Previously `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` returned the token object itself. After the first token refresh, every Google Calendar credential in the DB becomes `{success: true, data: {...}}`; the next `GoogleCalendarService` construction calls `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` which throws, breaking Google Calendar (and Google Meet) for the user until they reconnect. This happens in all modes, not just when credential syncing is enabled. The callers in office365/zoom/salesforce correctly use `.data`; Google must do the same (`key: parsed.data`).

findings.title: `prisma` used without being imported in Salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: The new refresh-and-persist logic calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` but the file never imports `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma` (the import list only has jsforce, rrule, zod, lib helpers, types, `getAppKeysFromSlug` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`). This is a TypeScript error and, if it ever ran, a `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` on every Salesforce service instantiation, making the Salesforce integration unusable. Add `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma";`.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys evaluate to "[object Object]" and strip every field except access_token
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` do not create wildcard keys; `ZodType` has no custom `toString`, so both evaluate to the literal key `"[object Object]"` (the second overwriting the first). The resulting schema is effectively `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`, and because `z.object` strips unknown keys, in sync mode `data` contains only `access_token` (plus the injected placeholder `refresh_token`). Consequences: Zoom computes `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = NaN which is persisted as `null` and makes `zoomTokenSchema.parse(credential.key)` fail on the next call; Office365 never gets a new `expires_in` so it refreshes on every request; Salesforce loses `instance_url`/`id`/`signature` from the stored key so the next connection has `instanceUrl: undefined`. Use `.passthrough()`/`.catchall(z.unknown())` and explicitly handle expiry rather than computed keys.

findings.title: Sync mode returns a raw fetch Response while several callers expect SDK-specific response shapes
findings.body: When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the `fetch` `Response` object regardless of what the wrapped `refreshFunction` would have returned. Several integrations were converted assuming the original shape: Google expects a gaxios response and reads `res.data.access_token` (undefined → TypeError, swallowed by the catch, so the stale expired auth is returned and calls fail); HubSpot expects a `HubspotToken` object and reads `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` then stores the `Response` object as the credential key; Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin expect an axios response and read `tokenInfo.data.error` (TypeError). So for Google Calendar, HubSpot, Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin the credential-sync feature cannot work at all, and in some cases corrupts the stored key. Either normalize the sync response to JSON and adapt each caller, or make the sync branch return the same shape as the provider SDK.

findings.title: appStoreMetadata is keyed by app directory name, not slug, so the webhook 404s for most apps
findings.body: `appStoreMetadata` (from `apps.metadata.generated.ts`) is keyed by the app's directory name (`googlecalendar`, `office365calendar`, `zoomvideo`, `office365video`, `larkcalendar`, ...), not by `slug` (`google-calendar`, `office365-calendar`, `zoom`, `msteams`, `lark-calendar`). The handler looks up `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]` after confirming the slug exists in the `App` table, so for every app whose dirName differs from its slug the lookup is `undefined` and the request returns 404 "App not found. Ensure that you have the correct app slug" even though the slug is correct. Only apps where dirName === slug (hubspot, salesforce, zohocrm, webex, zoho-bigin) work. Use `getAppFromSlug(slug)` from `@calcom/app-store/utils` (which searches by `slug`) instead.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes the credential id as the user id to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` — the third parameter is `userId: number | null` and is sent to the self-hoster's sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. `refreshAccessToken(credentialId, credentialKey)` only has the credential id in scope, so the sync endpoint will receive a credential id and return (or fail to return) tokens for the wrong user. Every other integration passes `credential.userId`; this method needs access to the credential's `userId` as well.

findings.title: Injected placeholder refresh_token overwrites the real refresh token stored in the DB
findings.body: When the parsed response lacks `refresh_token`, the function sets `data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers then merge this into the stored credential: Zoom does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` and Office365 does `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`. In sync mode (where the self-hoster is told to return only access token and expiry) this replaces the user's real refresh token in Cal.com's DB with the literal string `"refresh_token"`, so if syncing is later disabled or the endpoint is unavailable the credential is permanently unusable without reconnecting. In non-sync mode Office365's `refresh_token` is optional in `refreshTokenResponseSchema`, so a response without it would also destroy the stored token (previously the spread simply left the existing value untouched). Do not fabricate a refresh token; leave the field absent so callers keep the existing value.

findings.title: Request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT carries no authentication
findings.body: The POST to the self-hoster's credential sync endpoint sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` as form fields with no secret, signature or bearer token. The endpoint must return live OAuth access tokens for arbitrary users, so unless the self-hoster adds out-of-band protection (network allowlisting), anyone who discovers the URL can obtain any user's third-party access tokens by posting a user id. The inbound webhook already has `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`/`CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`; the outbound call should at minimum send the same secret header so the endpoint can authenticate Cal.com.

findings.title: Salesforce now refreshes on every instantiation, uses fragile statusText check, and connects with the stale access token
findings.body: `getClient` previously just constructed a `jsforce.Connection` (jsforce refreshes lazily on 401). It now unconditionally POSTs to `login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` every time the service is constructed (every booking, availability check, etc.), adding latency and a Salesforce API call per operation. The success check `response.statusText !== "OK"` is unreliable (status text is optional/empty for HTTP/2 and some proxies); use `response.ok`. After persisting the new token, the connection is still created with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` (the old one) instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, so the refresh result isn't even used for the current request. Also, the refresh does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so in sync mode Salesforce still contacts Salesforce directly while every other app contacts the self-hoster, which contradicts the feature's intent.

findings.title: Sync request uses "zoomvideo" while the webhook requires the DB slug "zoom"
findings.body: The `appSlug` sent to the credential sync endpoint for Zoom is the directory name `"zoomvideo"`, but the inbound `/api/webhook/app-credential` endpoint validates `appSlug` against `App.slug` in the DB, which is `"zoom"`. Other apps send their real slug (`google-calendar`, `office365-calendar`, `msteams`, `lark-calendar`). Self-hosters implementing the sync endpoint will have to special-case Zoom. Use `"zoom"` for consistency.

findings.title: Webex and Lark refresh paths route through the sync endpoint but keep provider-specific strict response validation
findings.body: Webex now calls `refreshOAuthTokens` (so in sync mode the response comes from the self-hoster) but still validates with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema`, which requires `scope` to be the exact literal `"spark:kms meeting:schedules_read meeting:schedules_write"`, `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`. Lark similarly passes the sync response through `handleLarkError`, which expects Lark's `{ code: 0, data: { access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in } }` envelope. The comment in `refreshOAuthTokens` tells self-hosters the response "should only contain the access token and expiry date", so a conforming endpoint will be rejected by both apps. Either use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (once fixed) in these apps or document the full provider-shaped response they require.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==` and no method restriction
findings.body: The shared secret is checked with a plain string inequality, which is vulnerable in principle to timing side channels; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers (as other webhook handlers in the repo do for signatures). The handler also accepts any HTTP method (GET included) and will read `req.body`; it should reject non-POST requests with 405.

findings.title: Body validation and decryption errors surface as unhandled 500s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a `ZodError` on malformed input, and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throws on a wrong key or non-JSON payload. Neither is caught, so the self-hoster receives a generic 500 with no indication of what was wrong. Use `safeParse` and wrap decryption in a try/catch, returning 400 with a message.

findings.title: Updating an existing credential does not clear the `invalid` flag
findings.body: Google Calendar and Zoom/Webex mark a credential `invalid: true` when the provider returns `invalid_grant`. When the parent application pushes fresh keys via this webhook, the update only sets `key`, so a previously invalidated credential stays flagged invalid and the UI/booking flows continue to treat it as broken even though it now has working tokens. The update should also set `invalid: false`.

findings.title: No tests for the new webhook or the shared refresh/parse utilities
findings.body: The PR adds a new public API route and two shared OAuth utilities used by ~10 integrations, and modifies the token-refresh path of every OAuth app, but ships no tests (the checklist explicitly says none were added). Even a minimal unit test of `parseRefreshTokenResponse` would have caught that the computed-key schema strips all fields, and an integration test of the Google refresh path would have caught the SafeParseReturnType being stored as the credential key. Please add unit tests for `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens` (both branches), and the webhook handler (auth failure, unknown slug, create vs update).
